proposals.relationship: Pagden uses Pocock’s account of political languages as distinguishable language-games to explain how historians reconstruct an argument’s vocabularies, conventions and intelligibility.
proposals.evidence_note: Pagden’s own opening discussion explicitly names and uses Pocock’s formulation. The publisher’s substantive opening excerpt was read; the complete 1987 introduction and Pocock’s chapter were not freshly read. This is a particular methodological resource, not influence inferred from the editorship or the whole Cambridge school. The print contribution is 1987; 2009 is the online publication date.
primary_locators: The Languages of Political Theory in Early-Modern Europe (1987), Introduction, public publisher excerpt under Summary, final two sentences naming Pocock; chapter pp. 1–18. Exact printed page of the unpaginated excerpt is not asserted.

proposals.relationship: Pagden adopts Todorov’s contrast between Spanish initiative and Mexica efforts to maintain the status quo in his particular interpretation of the first sustained encounter, and acknowledges Todorov’s suggestions for improving his work.
proposals.evidence_note: Pagden’s introduction, p. lv and note 43, explicitly identifies Todorov’s point; acknowledgments p. vi credit Todorov alongside Richard Kagan and Ángel Delgado Gómez. This is a scoped use and named feedback, not endorsement of every part of Todorov’s conquest thesis or a general claim about Indigenous passivity. Hernán Cortés is the letters’ author; Pagden is translator, editor and introduction author; J. H. Elliott’s introductory essay is separate. Pages were read in the 2001 Yale Nota Bene edition of a work first published in 1971 and revised in 1986. The witness is not backdated to 1971, and the date of each introductory revision is not independently established. Todorov’s original book and the complete letters remain unread.
primary_locators: Hernán Cortés, Letters from Mexico, 2001 Yale Nota Bene edition: title and copyright leaves; acknowledgments p. vi (PDF 11); Pagden Introduction p. lv, opening paragraph and note 43 (PDF 60).

proposals.relationship: Armitage credits Pagden with formative questions and continuing support for the doctoral study that developed into The Ideological Origins of the British Empire.
proposals.evidence_note: Armitage’s own acknowledgments p. x explicitly group Pagden with Chris Bayly, Peter Burke, Patrick Collinson and Istvan Hont in this Cambridge phase. All retain credit. This supports the named research contribution, not sole supervision, a particular question whose wording is unknown, or an inference from first meeting or institutional membership. Selected acknowledgments and publication leaves were read; Armitage’s full monograph remains unread.
primary_locators: The Ideological Origins of the British Empire (2000), acknowledgments p. x, second paragraph; publication/copyright leaf confirms 2000.

proposals.relationship: Thomas’s review identifies Taylor as a specific target of Pagden’s defense of Enlightenment cosmopolitanism against communitarian restrictions on moral judgment.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicitly mediated by Keith Thomas’s 2014 review of The Enlightenment: And Why It Still Matters (2013), in the paragraphs on communitarian adversaries. The localist and moral-relativist characterization is Pagden’s position as reported by Thomas, not an editorial judgment that it accurately exhausts Taylor’s philosophy. Alasdair MacIntyre retains co-target credit; no response by Taylor is inferred. Pagden’s original book and Taylor’s underlying works were not freshly read.
primary_locators: The Great Fight Over the Enlightenment, NYRB, 3 April 2014: paragraphs beginning His other adversaries and In opposition to the moral relativism; surrounding discussion of cosmopolitanism and human rights read. Unpaginated public text.

proposals.relationship: A comparison of the positions juxtaposed in The New Imperial Histories Reader contrasts Pagden’s rejection of an American-empire label with Chatterjee’s argument that the new global order is imperial.
proposals.evidence_note: An editorial teaching comparison grounded in Barbara Bush’s 2010 substantive review, which explicitly identifies these opposed positions in the reader’s final section. Stephen Howe is the reader’s editor. The comparison is undirected: it does not assert a personal reply, direct encounter, influence, or agreement across every definition of empire. The two original contributions and the complete reader were not freshly read; the positions remain attributed to Bush’s account of their juxtaposition.
primary_locators: Barbara Bush, review 989, The New Imperial Histories Reader (1 November 2010), paragraph beginning His essay challenges, followed by the paragraph naming Pagden and Chatterjee in the final colonial-present section.
